title: Earth system governance

definition.text: A field of research that places environmental policy and conservation in the wider context of human-caused change to the whole Earth system.

facts.text: In simple terms, it is the mix of rules and efforts by actors at every level, from local to global, that aim to prevent, reduce and adapt to environmental change.
It draws on political science, sociology, economics, ecology, policy studies, geography, sustainability science and law.
Its research is organised around five linked problems: architecture, agency, adaptiveness, accountability and legitimacy, and allocation and access.
Four cross-cutting themes run through these problems: power, knowledge, norms and scale; all levels of governance matter, not only the global one.
The idea was developed by Frank Biermann in a lecture published in 2007, and the global Earth System Governance Project began in 2009.
Critics say it is too top-down; Mike Hulme argues it is hubristic to try to control the global climate through universal governance regimes.

contested_note: Some critics call earth system governance too top-down and hubristic, while others say that reading of the concept is too narrow.

definition.text: A view of justice that extends environmental justice to the whole human and non-human world, covering fairness among people and between people and nature.

facts.text: Scholars called for planetary justice as early as 1972.
Five main approaches to planetary stewardship are market liberal, bioenvironmentalist, ecomodernist, institutionalist and social green, and none yet delivers a pro-poor vision of justice.

definition.text: A young legal field, part of earth system governance, that imagines law rooted in the planetary scale of the Anthropocene and its socio-ecological crisis.

facts.text: As of 2021 the concept was still in its infancy, and its precise content, purpose and scope remain a work in progress.

definition.text: An approach to environmental governance that builds cooperation among actors across scales and jurisdictions to deal with mismatches of scale in linked human and natural systems.

facts.text: Collaboration can create new knowledge through social learning, in which what individuals learn by interacting changes a whole community's understanding.
It can bring Indigenous and traditional knowledge into decisions, which may raise trust and the sense that the process is fair.
Collaboration costs time and resources and can be too slow for urgent problems.
Where large state actors dominate, collaboration can become co-optation that reinforces uneven power.

title: Ecosystem-based management

definition.text: An environmental management approach that considers all the interactions within an ecosystem, humans included, instead of single issues, species or ecosystem services in isolation.

facts.text: Its roots lie in the Great Lakes ecosystem policy of the late 1970s and the 1978 Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement, built on the claim that 'no park is an island'.
In 1932 an Ecological Society of America committee argued that US national parks had to protect all the ecosystems they contained, ideas that became its foundation.
The Craigheads found in 1979 that Yellowstone's grizzly bears could not survive within park boundaries alone, supporting broader ecosystem definitions.
Goals must cover social, cultural and economic values, not only scientific ones, and communities and stakeholders must be involved throughout.
In the oceans it moves away from single-species or single-sector management toward weighing all the human activities that affect marine environments.
Because linked social-ecological systems cannot be fully predicted or controlled, an adaptive management approach is recommended.
Scientific consensus now favours ecosystem-based fisheries management as the most viable way to balance human needs and keep ecosystem services.

contested_note: A debate continues over whether ecosystem-based management has been fully put into practice.

definition.text: The ways decisions are made about controlling and managing the environment and natural resources, involving government, business and civil society.

facts.text: Key principles include building the environment into every level of decision-making and treating cities, economic and political life as part of the environment.
It also promotes a shift from open-loop, cradle-to-grave systems toward closed-loop, cradle-to-cradle systems such as zero-waste strategies.
Challenges include weak global agreements, poor coordination among the UN, governments, business and civil society, and an imbalance with trade and finance bodies such as the WTO.
The time lag between human action and environmental effect can be as long as a generation.
Since the 1970s many new international institutions have appeared, causing overlap and fragmentation but also chances for cooperation.
A 2018 study of 461 waterbird species at more than 25,000 sites found strong environmental governance was one of the most reliable predictors of conservation success.
Local governance stresses community participation and decentralisation, a bottom-up departure from earlier state-driven, top-down approaches.

definition.text: The match, or mismatch, between the scale of an environmental problem and the level at which policy tackles it.

facts.text: Such mismatches reduce how well interventions work.
Elinor Ostrom and others argued that mismatch often causes unsustainable management and that no simple fixes have been found.
Collaborative environmental governance aims to deal with scale mismatches in social-ecological systems.

title: Fisheries co-management

definition.text: A flexible, cooperative way of managing aquatic resources in which fishing communities and government share responsibility.

facts.text: Five types are recognised by how power is shared: instructive, consultative, cooperative, advisory and informative management, running from government-led to user-led.
It arose because top-down fisheries management often failed and communities ignored rules, such as cuts in total allowable catch, that they did not understand.
Unlike community management, the government takes part in decisions, and rules are made and enforced jointly.
It combines scientific and traditional knowledge, and users who agree to rules are more likely to obey and help enforce them.
It is slow and costly, and some argue it empowers the already wealthy and powerful.

contested_note: Some argue co-management entrenches existing inequalities, while others see it as a means of empowering communities.

title: Adaptive management

definition.text: A structured, repeated process for making decisions under uncertainty that uses monitoring to learn and reduce that uncertainty over time.

facts.text: Each decision serves management goals while also gathering information that improves future management.
Its main features are iterative decisions, feedback between monitoring and decisions, and treating uncertainty as a way to build understanding.
Passive adaptive management values learning only for better outcomes, while active adaptive management builds learning into the objective itself.
The hard part is balancing learning for the future against the best short-term result from current knowledge.
C. S. Holling and C. J. Walters at the University of British Columbia developed the approach and distinguished its passive and active forms.
In conservation it has three parts: testing assumptions, adapting interventions to monitoring results, and documenting lessons for learning.
Its effectiveness is hard to test, because one cannot see how another approach would have done in exactly the same situation.
Each decision both pursues management goals and gathers information to improve future management.

notes: C. S. Holling founder status is decided in the people chapter.; S:eba28ccea125 carries a CONTESTED flag from the word 'uncertain'; not a real debate.

title: Bloomington school

definition.text: A research tradition in political economy, built around Elinor and Vincent Ostrom at Indiana University Bloomington, that studies how institutions and communities govern shared problems.

facts.text: It focuses on governance, collective action and institutional diversity, especially for common-pool resources, decentralisation and self-governance.
The Ostroms founded its home, the Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis, in 1973.
Elinor Ostrom's Governing the Commons (1990) challenged the 'tragedy of the commons' by showing communities worldwide managing common-pool resources successfully.
Her research named eight design principles for successful commons, among them clear boundaries, collective decisions, monitoring, graduated sanctions and conflict resolution.
Elinor Ostrom won the 2009 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, the first woman to receive it.
Critics say its findings are hard to scale up to national or global levels and that it underplays power and inequality.

contested_note: Some economists doubt Ostrom's commons findings scale up, and critical scholars say the school neglects power and inequality.

title: Polycentric governance

definition.text: Governance by many overlapping, independent decision-making centres operating at different scales, rather than by one central authority.

facts.text: Vincent Ostrom argued such systems can improve efficiency, accountability and problem-solving.
It challenged the usual choice between central government control and privatisation, suggesting self-organising systems often beat top-down solutions.
Elinor Ostrom proposed that key management decisions be taken as close as possible to the events and actors involved.
Some question whether it works where institutions are weak or corruption is high.
In a polycentric network, a resource that cannot be monitored as a whole is less likely to be well managed, as with space debris.

contested_note: Critics question whether polycentric governance applies where institutional capacity is weak or corruption is high.
notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own.

definition.text: A process for managing coasts sustainably that works across geographic and political boundaries and weighs natural, social and economic systems together.

facts.text: The concept was developed at the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio and set out in Chapter 17 of Agenda 21.
Coastal margins cover 8% of the world's surface but provide 25% of global resources, and about 70% of people live within a day's walk of the coast.
It runs in five steps: situation assessment, plan, institutionalisation of the plan, implementation and ongoing evaluation, with no end state.
Its main constraints are institutional rather than technological, and treating the coast as common property hampers top-down control.

definition.text: The diplomacy, mechanisms and responses aimed at steering societies to prevent, mitigate or adapt to the risks of climate change.

facts.text: Modern international climate governance rests on three pillars: mitigation, adaptation and means of implementation.
A defining milestone was the 1992 UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, which sought to copy the Montreal Protocol's success with ozone.
Under the 2015 Paris Agreement each country submits its own nationally determined contribution, which is not legally binding.
The North–South divide between high-emitting developed countries and low-emitting developing ones underlies the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities.
It works across supranational, national, regional and local scales, with cities, NGOs, firms and courts as actors alongside states.
It increasingly relies on market mechanisms, such as the Kyoto Protocol's emissions trading, clean development mechanism and joint implementation, alongside command-and-control rules.
A country that stays out of an agreement can still benefit from others' emission cuts without acting itself.

title: Aarhus Convention

definition.text: A 1998 UNECE treaty, signed in Aarhus, Denmark, that gives the public rights to environmental information, participation in decisions and access to justice.

facts.text: It rests on three pillars: access to information, public participation in decision-making, and access to justice when environmental law is broken.
It entered into force in 2001, and in April 2023 had 49 parties, 48 states and the European Union, almost all in Europe and Central Asia.
It binds public authorities but excludes the private sector, whose disclosure stays voluntary.
Its compliance mechanism is unique in international environmental law because members of the public can complain directly to a committee of legal experts.
Its Kyiv Protocol is the first legally binding international instrument on pollutant release and transfer registers, inventories of pollution from industry and other sources.
Kofi Annan called it the most impressive elaboration of Principle 10 of the Rio Declaration on citizen participation.
Critics say its focus on procedures over outcomes makes it vague, and that ordinary citizens often lack the means to take part.

related: Rio Declaration on Environment and Development
contested_note: Critics question whether NGOs faithfully represent citizens under the convention and whether its procedural focus leaves it too vague.

title: Agenda 21

definition.text: A non-binding United Nations action plan for sustainable development, produced by the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro.

facts.text: 178 governments voted to adopt it at the Earth Summit in June 1992.
Its four sections cover social and economic dimensions, conservation and management of resources, the role of major groups, and means of implementation.
It is meant to be carried out at local, national and global levels, and every local government is expected to draw up its own local Agenda 21.
Implementation by member states is voluntary and has varied.
The 2015 Sustainable Development Goals took its goals and reaffirmed them as the basis of sustainable development, in 17 goals.
In the United States it became the target of conspiracy theories claiming a UN plot against property rights and sovereignty.

related: Rio Declaration on Environment and Development

definition.text: Local programmes in which towns and cities carry out Agenda 21's sustainable development plan, as its Chapter 28 recommends.

facts.text: The Rio+10 report found over 6400 local governments in 113 countries engaged in Local Agenda 21, and 5120 of them were in Europe.
Sweden reported that 100% of its municipalities had adopted it by 2002.
ICLEI-Local Governments for Sustainability, formed in 1990, is widely seen as a model of Agenda 21 implementation.

definition.text: An international treaty that limits the movement of hazardous waste between countries, especially from developed to less developed countries.

facts.text: It was opened for signature on 21 March 1989, entered into force on 5 May 1992, and had 191 parties as of June 2024.
It arose because tighter laws in rich countries in the 1970s made waste disposal costly, so hazardous waste trade to poorer countries grew rapidly.
A trigger was the Khian Sea incident, in which a ship carrying Philadelphia incinerator ash dumped half its load on a beach in Haiti.
It requires notice, consent and tracking for cross-border waste shipments and aims to manage waste as close to its source as possible, giving an incentive to cut waste.
In May 2019 it was amended to include plastic waste as a regulated material, though the United States, a non-party, opposed this.
It calls illegal hazardous waste traffic criminal but contains no enforcement provisions.

title: Basel Ban Amendment

definition.text: A 1995 amendment to the Basel Convention that bans exports of hazardous waste from mostly OECD developed countries to developing countries, for any reason including recycling.

facts.text: It came because the original convention only required prior informed consent and traders were justifying exports as recycling.
Croatia became the 97th country to ratify it on 6 September 2019, so it entered into force on 5 December 2019.
Industry groups and countries including Australia and Canada strongly opposed it.

contested_note: Parties disagreed over how many ratifications were needed for the amendment to enter into force.

definition.text: The use of lawsuits to set legal precedents that push governments and companies to act on climate change.

facts.text: It grew as activists and lawyers turned to courts because climate politics was slow to deliver mitigation.
Cases usually rest on one of five kinds of claim: constitutional, administrative, private law, fraud or consumer protection, or human rights.
Cases rose from 884 in 24 countries in 2017 to at least 1,550 in 38 countries by July 2020, most of them in the United States.
In the Urgenda case, Dutch courts ordered the government to cut carbon dioxide emissions by 25% from 1990 levels by the end of 2020.
In 2021 a Hague court ordered Royal Dutch Shell to cut its global carbon emissions by 45% by 2030 compared with 2019 levels, including scope 3 emissions.
In 2024 the European Court of Human Rights became the first international court to rule that state inaction on climate change violates human rights.
Results are mixed, and companies may answer successful cases with 'backlash' suits, such as RWE's claim against the Netherlands under the Energy Charter Treaty.

title: Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution
article: Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution

definition.text: A UNECE treaty that commits its parties to limit, gradually reduce and prevent air pollution, including pollution that travels long distances across borders.

facts.text: It opened for signature on 13 November 1979 and entered into force on 16 March 1983; it now has 51 parties.
Eight protocols set specific emission cuts, including the 1985 Helsinki Protocol on sulphur and the 1999 Gothenburg Protocol on acidification, eutrophication and ground-level ozone.
It was an early international effort to protect the atmosphere as a global commons, and is listed among the treaties used against acid rain.

definition.text: A framework under the Convention on Biological Diversity for the integrated management of land, water and living resources that promotes conservation and fair, sustainable use.

facts.text: It brings people, the economy and ecology together into the solution of a given problem.
It became a central topic for the Convention on Biological Diversity at its second Conference of the Parties in November 1995.
At the fifth Conference of the Parties, the parties asked their scientific advisory body for a description of the approach with 12 principles.
Ecosystem management and ecosystem-based management are close relatives; all three aim to conserve and protect ecosystems but differ in framework and methods.
Applied to fisheries, it becomes the ecosystem approach to fisheries, which builds local strategies for each fishery ecosystem.

title: Ecosystem management

definition.text: An approach to natural resource management that aims to keep an ecosystem's functions and services going over the long term while meeting people's social, economic, political and cultural needs.

facts.text: Indigenous communities practised it implicitly for millennia, but it became a formal concept in the 1990s; the US Forest Service chief F. Dale Robertson formalised the term in 1992.
Unlike command-and-control management, which often weakens ecological resilience, it is holistic and adaptive.
Industrial societies had managed ecosystems mainly to maximise yields of one resource, as when US fire suppression led to fuel buildup and more intense fires.
A core principle is that long-term production of goods and services is a precondition for management, not an afterthought.
It is carried out through adaptive management, strategic management and landscape-scale conservation, with broad stakeholder participation.
It remains ambiguous and controversial, partly because some formulations rest on contested policy and scientific claims.

contested_note: Ecosystem management is described as ambiguous and controversial because some formulations rest on contested claims.

title: European Green Deal

definition.text: A set of European Commission policies, approved in 2020, whose overarching aim is to make the European Union climate neutral by 2050.

facts.text: It reviews every existing law on its climate merits and adds new laws on the circular economy, building renovation, biodiversity, farming and innovation.
It includes carbon tariffs on countries that cut emissions more slowly, through the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism.
Its parts include a Farm to Fork food strategy, a Zero Pollution Action Plan, the EU Biodiversity Strategy and the binding Nature Restoration Law.
A Just Transition Mechanism gives more financial aid to countries with more coal and oil shale workers or higher emissions.
In 2017 more than 75% of EU greenhouse gas emissions came from producing and using energy.
Critics say it falls short of ending fossil fuels, while others blame it for higher energy prices, lost competitiveness and farmer protests.

contested_note: Environmental groups call the deal too weak, while some governments, industries and farmers oppose its costs and timeline.

definition.text: A non-binding 1992 Earth Summit document setting out recommendations for conserving and sustainably developing all types of forests.

facts.text: Negotiations were complicated by developing nations in the Group of 77 seeking more aid to pay for forest reserves, and the final text was a compromise.
They linked deforestation to third world debt and poor technology transfer, and said the extra cost of forest conservation should be shared equitably.
They led to the Montréal Process on criteria and indicators for temperate and boreal forests in 1994.

definition.text: The institutions that coordinate the behaviour of actors across borders, help them cooperate, settle disputes and ease collective-action problems.

facts.text: It means making, monitoring and enforcing rules among interdependent actors when there is no overarching political authority.
Many kinds of actors, not only states, exercise power within it, including intergovernmental bodies, NGOs, businesses and civil society.
The League of Nations, founded in 1920, was one of the first organisations to promote it.
Its arrangements may be formal laws and institutions, or informal practices, guidelines and coalitions.
Treaty secretariats, such as that of the UN climate convention, have significant influence but cannot enforce laws.
Governance for sustainability is highly fragmented: a 2022 study counted 335 international organisations in the field, often weakly connected and competing for resources.

definition.text: A way of governing globally through goals that are not legally binding, leave each country flexibility and come without strong institutions.

facts.text: The Sustainable Development Goals for 2015 to 2030 are an example, following the Millennium Development Goals of 2000 to 2015.

definition.text: A soft, indirect form of global steering in which an actor such as an international organisation recruits voluntary intermediaries to influence a target group.

facts.text: It fills gaps by complementing existing regimes; its three activities are agenda setting, coordination and support.
The UN's five regional economic commissions act as orchestrators for the Sustainable Development Goals.

definition.text: The worldwide system of institutions and agreements that tackles transboundary environmental problems such as climate change, biodiversity loss and land degradation.

facts.text: A 2020 publication called it one of the most institutionally dynamic areas of world politics over the previous thirty years.
As of 2020 the International Environmental Agreement Database counted almost 1300 multilateral and over 2200 bilateral agreements.
Policy made separately by theme, sector or territory has produced treaties that overlap or clash.
UNEP coordinates environmental responses within the UN but is widely considered a weak organisation.
Some Global South countries see environmental governance as a 'luxury' priority of the Global North that conflicts with economic development.

definition.text: A treaty among countries, meant to be legally binding, whose main purpose is to prevent or manage human impacts on natural resources.

facts.text: An agreement between two nations is bilateral; one among three or more is a multilateral environmental agreement (MEA).
The first MEA, in 1857, regulated water flowing from Lake Constance to Austria and Switzerland; 747 MEAs were concluded between 1857 and 2012.
They multiplied after the 1972 Stockholm Conference, whose declaration was the first universal document of importance on an environmental issue.
Tools for effectiveness include trade sanctions against non-signatories and funds to share costs, such as the Montreal Protocol's $240 million fund.
Differential obligations, as in the Kyoto Protocol, give countries different targets based mainly on their development and can widen participation.
Because sovereignty means no country can be forced to join, a country facing economic costs may shirk while others comply, a classic free-rider problem.
They are criticised as slow, tending to the lowest common denominator, and lacking monitoring and enforcement.

title: Law of the sea

definition.text: The body of international law setting out the rights and duties of states at sea, from navigation to seabed minerals and coastal waters.

facts.text: It derives mainly from the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, in force since 1994 and sometimes called the 'constitution of the oceans'.
In 1945 US President Truman extended American jurisdiction to the natural resources of its continental shelf, and Chile, Peru and Ecuador soon claimed 200 nautical miles.
UNCLOS gives each state an exclusive economic zone of 200 nautical miles with exclusive rights to fisheries, minerals and seabed deposits.
As of June 2019 UNCLOS had been ratified by 168 states, and non-parties such as the US still treat its provisions as customary law.
It is enforced through bodies such as the International Seabed Authority and the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea in Hamburg.
About 64% of the world's oceans are international waters subject to the Law of the Sea.

related: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea

title: Freedom of the seas

definition.text: The principle that the open sea is international territory that every nation may use but none may own.

facts.text: Hugo Grotius set it out in Mare Liberum in 1609, arguing the sea, like air, cannot be occupied and is meant for everyone's use.
John Selden replied in Mare Clausum that the sea could be appropriated by states just like land.
National waters were long limited to a belt of usually three nautical miles under the 'cannon shot' rule.
The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea replaced the older freedom-of-the-seas concept.

contested_note: Grotius argued the sea is common to all, while Selden argued it could be owned like land.

definition.text: Six principles set out in 1997 by ecological economist Robert Costanza for the sustainable governance of the oceans and other shared resources.

facts.text: Access to environmental resources brings a duty to use them in ways that are ecologically sustainable, economically efficient and socially fair.
Under uncertainty about irreversible harm, decisions should err on the side of caution, and the burden of proof should fall on those whose activities may cause damage.
All internal and external costs and benefits should be identified and allocated, and markets adjusted to reflect full costs where appropriate.
Governance should sit at scales that have the best information and can act quickly, and all stakeholders should take part.

title: London Convention on marine dumping
article: London Convention on the Prevention of Marine Pollution by Dumping of Wastes and Other Matter

definition.text: A 1972 treaty to control pollution of the sea from the deliberate dumping of wastes from ships, aircraft and platforms.

facts.text: It entered into force on 30 August 1975 and uses a 'black list' of banned materials and a 'grey list' needing special care.
Its 1996 Protocol codified the precautionary approach and the polluter pays principle, and switched to a 'reverse list' banning any dumping not explicitly allowed.
In 2013 parties to the London Protocol adopted a legally binding framework for regulating marine geoengineering, starting with ocean fertilisation.
It does not cover land-based sources such as pipes and outfalls.

definition.text: A public process of mapping and allocating where and when human activities take place at sea to meet ecological, economic and social goals set through politics.

facts.text: It is similar to land-use planning, but for marine waters, and generally uses maps of how an area is used and what resources and habitats it holds.
Planning lets managers weigh the combined effects of maritime industries and reduce conflicts between users of the same sea area.
Its aim is to use marine resources within clear environmental limits so ecosystems stay healthy and biodiversity is conserved.
The EU's Maritime Spatial Planning Directive required coastal member states to set up their own plans by 2021, covering fishing, aquaculture, conservation, shipping and renewable energy.
It can speed offshore renewable energy by streamlining licensing and reducing conflict among sea users.

definition.text: The way power is spread vertically across levels of government and horizontally across many non-state and quasi-state organisations.

facts.text: Liesbet Hooghe and Gary Marks developed the concept in the early 1990s from studying the structures the EU created under the 1992 Maastricht Treaty.
It describes authority shifting both up from central states to bodies like the EU and down to subnational authorities.
The vertical dimension links higher and lower levels of government; the horizontal dimension covers cooperation between regions or municipalities.
Cities may contribute up to 75% of global carbon dioxide emissions, so national climate targets depend on local and subnational action.
Critics say the idea of 'levels' implies a hierarchy, when real levels interact in complex, non-hierarchical ways.

title: National park

definition.text: A government-owned and protected area of natural, semi-natural or developed land set aside for conservation because of its outstanding national natural, historic or cultural value.

facts.text: Yellowstone, established by the United States in 1872, is widely held to be the world's first national park.
The IUCN classes national parks as Category II protected areas; in 1971 its criteria included a minimum size of 1,000 hectares and a ban on exploiting natural resources.
Many countries use the term loosely; in the UK a national park is a scenic, lightly developed area with planning limits and may contain sizeable settlements.
Parks Canada, set up in 1911, is the world's oldest national park service, and Canada has 450,000 km2 of national park space.
Parks support nature-based tourism; in Costa Rica park tourism rose by 400% from 1985 to 1999.
Critics say parks in former colonies removed native communities and reinforce the idea that nature is protected only where people are absent.

contested_note: Critics see national parks in former colonies as a form of eco-land grabbing that displaced native communities.

title: Public participation

definition.text: Involving the public, especially those affected by or interested in a decision, in the activities and decisions of an organisation or project.

facts.text: Its core principle is that people affected by a decision have a right to take part in making it.
It is more inclusive than stakeholder engagement and implies that public input can change outcomes.
It is recognised as an environmental principle and enshrined in the Rio Declaration.
Because government alone cannot solve environmental problems, involving the public can improve transparency, accountability and compliance with environmental law.
Low-income citizens often struggle to take part because of childcare costs, time off work and limited access to education on public matters.
The hoped-for gains in public trust from participation have yet to be confirmed.

related: Rio Declaration on Environment and Development

title: Race to the bottom

definition.text: A situation in which governments, firms or individuals compete by steadily lowering standards or regulations to cut costs and attract economic activity.

facts.text: Unlike ordinary competition, which tends to improve goods and services, it erodes labour laws, tax rates and environmental rules.
Places with stricter labour or environmental rules or higher taxes can lose business to less regulated places, pushing them to lower their own standards.
The term traces to US Justice Louis Brandeis, describing states competing to attract corporations in the late 1800s and early 1900s.
Firms may move to countries that do not require them to treat chemical waste before dumping it, avoiding costly treatment.
Globalisation lets a producer unconcerned with biodiversity undercut one who cares, driving a race to the bottom in conservation rules.
Whether it really happens is debated: Daniel Drezner calls it a myth, and a 2022 study found no evidence of it in labour standards, though Nita Rudra found it in developing countries.
Some US states pursue the opposite, a 'race to the top', with innovative environmental policies other states may copy.

contested_note: Scholars disagree on whether a race to the bottom actually occurs, with empirical evidence on both sides.

title: Rio Conventions

definition.text: The three conventions agreed at the June 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro: on climate change (UNFCCC), biological diversity (CBD) and desertification (UNCCD).

facts.text: The summit also produced Agenda 21, the Forest Principles and the Rio Declaration.
The CBD's three objectives are conserving biodiversity, using its components sustainably and sharing fairly the benefits of genetic resources.
The UNFCCC aims to stabilise greenhouse gas concentrations at a level that prevents dangerous human interference with the climate system.
The UNCCD links sustainable land management to land degradation and aims at land degradation neutrality, with a focus on restoring drylands.

related: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification

title: Rio Declaration on Environment and Development
article: Rio Declaration on Environment and Development

definition.text: A short document of 27 principles, produced at the 1992 Earth Summit, to guide countries in future sustainable development.

facts.text: Its first principle says sustainable development is chiefly about people, who are entitled to healthy, productive lives in harmony with nature.
Principle 15 states the precautionary principle, to be applied by states according to their capabilities.
Principle 16 encourages the polluter pays principle where it serves the public interest and does not distort trade and investment.
Principle 10 stresses citizens' participation and access to environmental information, later elaborated by the Aarhus Convention.
It built on the 1972 Stockholm Declaration, aiming to set out principles states can write into their own laws.
It raised environmental awareness, but evidence from 2007 suggested little of its environmental goals had been achieved.

definition.text: Managing space and resources by making and carrying out plans that limit how land and space can be used and developed.

facts.text: It is usually done by national, regional or local governments and balances competing demands on land from the state, the market and local communities.
It is needed because the economy, housing and environmental protection all compete for space.
Its disciplines include land-use, urban, regional, transport and environmental planning, as well as maritime spatial planning.

definition.text: An ethical practice of responsibly planning and managing resources, which can be applied to the environment, economics, property and more.

facts.text: The word comes from the duties of a household steward, a keeper of the hall.
Natural resource management focuses on how management affects quality of life for present and future generations, which is called stewardship.
Stewardship councils certify products, such as the Forest Stewardship Council since 1993 and the Marine Stewardship Council since 1996.

definition.text: A governance approach that tries to speed up sustainability transitions through a participatory process of shared visions, learning and experiments.

facts.text: Participants meet in a 'transition arena' to define shared problems and visions, which are then tested through experiments and reflection.
It takes a long view of one to three generations and favours 'learn by doing, doing by learning' at the niche level.
Rather than control change by command and control, it steers and indirectly redirects actors' choices toward sustainability.
The Dutch government used it in the early 2000s to manage a radical transformation of its energy system.
With few case studies, its methodology is still debated.

definition.text: A framework that sees change in socio-technical systems as playing out across three levels: the broad landscape, the dominant regime and innovative niches.

facts.text: The landscape is the wider setting of values, beliefs, institutions and market conditions, and it changes slowly.
The regime is the set of dominant practices, rules and technologies that keep the current system stable.
Rising environmental awareness, a landscape change, pressures regimes such as aviation and agriculture and opens room for new technologies.

definition.text: Environmental policy that tackles global problems such as climate change, ozone depletion or marine pollution and involves actors from at least two sovereign states.

facts.text: As of 2018 more than 1,800 multilateral environmental agreements were in effect, more than 190 of them on climate change.
The 1972 Stockholm conference is seen as the beginning of international environmental law and policy.
Transnational environmental NGOs drive change through market-based certification, of which the Forest Stewardship Council is among the most successful.

title: Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer
article: Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer

definition.text: A 1985 multilateral agreement that set the framework for international cuts in chlorofluorocarbons, which destroy the ozone layer.

facts.text: Research in the 1970s showed that man-made CFCs, used in products such as refrigerators, break down atmospheric ozone.
It entered into force in 1988 and provided the framework for the binding Montreal Protocol, though it set no binding CFC cuts itself.
Ratified by 198 states and the European Union, it is one of the most universally accepted treaties ever.
A Multilateral Fund has aided projects in nearly 150 countries, preventing the use of roughly 250,000 tons of ozone-depleting chemicals.

definition.text: The management of how human societies interact with and affect the environment, rather than management of the environment itself.

facts.text: It aims to protect ecosystem services for future generations and keep ecosystems intact, weighing ethical, economic and ecological factors.
It links to natural resource, fisheries, forest and wildlife management and to environmental management systems.
The economy works within and depends on goods and services from natural ecosystems.
Its strategies rest on views of the human-nature relationship, from anthropocentrism, which values nature only for people, to ecocentrism, which grants nature intrinsic value.
ISO 14001 is the most widely used environmental management standard and is closely aligned with the EU's Eco-Management and Audit Scheme.
Resilience thinking calls for a shift from maximum sustainable yield toward environmental resource and ecosystem management.

title: Science–policy interface

definition.text: The meeting ground where scientists and policy-makers work together so that research can inform, and be guided by, decisions.

facts.text: IPBES was established by governments in 2012 to strengthen the science-policy interface for biodiversity and ecosystem services.
The IPCC was the first of three global science-policy panels, followed by IPBES in 2012 and a panel on chemicals, waste and pollution in 2025.
Translating research into governance is hard because science and politics treat uncertainty very differently.
A review of pollution found a lack of a globally supported formal science–policy interface to inform action, research and funding.

related: Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services

definition.text: The rules and agreements that govern how states share transboundary waters, meaning rivers, lakes, seas or groundwater bordered by two or more states.

facts.text: Countries negotiate transboundary water agreements to reduce the risk of conflict, but many shared international rivers still lack treaties.
Such agreements often focus on water infrastructure and water quality.
The UNECE Water Convention on transboundary watercourses and international lakes, signed in Helsinki in 1992, entered into force on 6 October 1996.
Its principles of 'prior appropriation' and 'riparianism' can worsen conflict by legally fixing who has water abundance and who has scarcity.

definition.text: Action taken together by a group of people to improve their condition and reach a common objective.

facts.text: The economic theory of collective action concerns providing public goods through the collaboration of two or more individuals; Mancur Olson's 1965 book The Logic of Collective Action is an early analysis of public-good costs.
Olson argued that individuals with more resources carry a higher burden of providing a public good, while poorer ones tend to free ride, which can lead to under-provision.

Institutional designs for public goods include joint products that tie a private good to a public good, clubs that exclude non-members, and federated structures, since collaboration emerges more easily in small groups.
The social identity model of collective action explains participation through perceived injustice, perceived efficacy and social identity.

definition.text: Research conducted with the participation of the general public or amateur and nonprofessional researchers.

facts.text: It is used in ecology, biology, conservation, health, astronomy and more; the term first appeared in a January 1989 MIT Technology Review issue on community labs studying environmental issues.
Projects are categorized by participants' involvement; at the low end, contributory or crowdsourcing projects have citizens collect observations, offer computing power or install sensors.
Citizen science has contributed much to biodiversity analysis, mostly species occurrence, abundance and phenology data, with birds the most observed group.
Smartphones and internet platforms vastly expanded participation, through apps such as iNaturalist and Mosquito Alert.
Ethics and data governance, including data protection law and community control over reuse, are growing concerns; ECSA published Ten Principles of Citizen Science in 2015.
Researchers have estimated the monetary value of citizen science contributions, for example from seven Zooniverse projects.

definition.text: Harmful effects in the ocean from substances humans use or spread, such as waste, particles, noise, light, excess carbon dioxide or invasive organisms.

facts.text: About 80% of the waste comes from land-based activity, with marine transportation also contributing; this makes continental shelves most vulnerable.
Pollution enters the sea by three main routes: direct discharge, runoff carried by rain, and release from the atmosphere.
Farm, urban and construction runoff carries nutrients that fuel algal blooms, which can use up oxygen and create hypoxic conditions.
Eighty percent of marine debris is plastic, which breaks down into microplastics and nanoplastics.
Persistent toxicants such as PCBs, DDT, dioxins and PFAS, and heavy metals such as mercury, lead, copper and cadmium, break down slowly or not at all.
Between 1950 and 2026 the average ocean surface pH fell from about 8.15 to 8.05, with human carbon dioxide emissions the primary cause.
Pollution can reduce marine biodiversity and productivity and deplete human marine food resources.

Early on, most scientists thought the oceans were so vast they could dilute pollution harmlessly; significant international laws came only in the twentieth century. SDG Target 14.1 aims to prevent and significantly reduce marine pollution by 2025.
